items.stem: Why should a choropleth usually map a rate rather than a raw count?

options.text: Raw counts largely track population size and can mislead; rates normalise for it
options.rationale: Correct: normalising to a rate removes the population-size artefact.
Magnitude is not the reason; comparability is.

options.text: Counts cannot be mapped at all
options.rationale: Counts can be mapped but often mislead on a choropleth.
Colour works for either; the issue is interpretation.

items.explanation: Correct: normalising to a rate removes the population-size artefact.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about coordinate reference systems are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Layers must share a coordinate system to align correctly
options.rationale: Correct: mismatched systems misregister the layers.

options.text: Distances should be measured in a projected metric system, not raw degrees
options.rationale: Correct: degrees are not a constant distance unit.

options.text: All projections preserve area, shape and distance at once
options.rationale: No single projection preserves all properties simultaneously.

items.explanation: Correct: mismatched systems misregister the layers.

items.stem: A report concludes individuals in high-income regions all buy a product, from region-level averages. What error is this?

options.text: The ecological fallacy: inferring individual behaviour from area averages
options.rationale: Correct: area-level patterns need not hold for individuals.
Autocorrelation describes similarity of nearby values, not this inference error.
The error is about aggregation, not projection.
It is not valid; it commits the ecological fallacy.

items.explanation: Correct: area-level patterns need not hold for individuals.
